P1-T011.notes: The authority rule is docs/architecture/CONFIG_AUTHORITY.md's sentence as code: a layer cannot widen what a layer above it allows, and cannot weaken a restriction a layer above it imposed. New file crates/sure-core/src/config/authority.rs. Layer is User and Project and nothing else -- rank 3 (organization policy) is not a variant, so no caller can name a source it can never obtain, and rank 1 (the person at the keyboard) is not configuration and stays in ConsentGrantor::InteractiveUser. Layer::can_grant is a match, not 'self == Self::User', so a third layer must answer the question. Authority::privileges() records every ask including refused ones -- request, every layer that asked (most trusted first), grantor or None -- because dropping refusals would make 'asked and refused' and 'never asked' the same list. A grant comes only from the topmost layer that asked and only if that layer may grant; a project and its user both asking is not an escalation. permissions() is not decide(): it says which permissions a file was allowed to hand over, and the execution mode is deliberately not a permission, so a project asking for host_confirmed gets nothing in the set. Restrictions resolve the other way -- protection and privacy take the stricter of the two layers with Resolved::by naming the most trusted layer that asked -- and 'by: None' means 'nothing beyond the default' rather than 'SURE did not look'. Ranks are hand-written matches rather than a derived Ord, with the two unavailable variants ranked in the safe direction. No merged Config (ADR 0011); scope reductions are reported, never overridden. Config::load split into load/load_file so the user's configuration is read by the same reader at a different path, with the sure.yml near-miss check following the file name -- now a contract of a public function, so it has its own test. P2-T002.notes: crates/sure-core/src/fingerprint/ (digest.rs, git/mod.rs, git/status.rs, error.rs, mod.rs) + tests/fingerprint_git.rs (34 tests on Windows, 37 on Unix) + docs/architecture/FINGERPRINTING.md; scan/ignore.rs gained left_out() so the fingerprint and the scan cannot disagree about which directories are out of scope. Acceptance criterion 1, HEAD/dirty tracked diff/relevant untracked state affect fingerprint: the digest is over the project's file contents, not over Git's diff, because a diff changes when the same files are committed, amended or rebased while the project state a check would read has not. HEAD is digested and the branch name is not -- the branch is recorded in GitState for a person to read, and two branches at the same commit are the same state. A deletion and an empty file are two states (the Gone arm writes a marker, not the digest of empty content). A clean project has no change digest at all, rather than the digest of an empty list, so clean and empty-list are two states and not one; the domain type says so with an Option and the code follows it. Acceptance criterion 2, fingerprint changes on relevant source changes: every change record contributes the file's own path and its contents, and the untracked tree is walked file by file. Digest framing: the domain tag sure.git-fingerprint.v1 is the first field, every field is written length-then-bytes so (ab,c) cannot hash equal to (a,bc), and an absent optional field writes a presence byte rather than an empty string. SHA-256, because the project being fingerprinted is written by a coding agent and an adversary choosing a collision is in scope, not hypothetical. Git is asked for status with --untracked-files=all --no-renames -- . plus a separate rev-parse --show-prefix. --relative is deliberately absent and is now forbidden by a comment and by a mutation: on this machine's Git 2.55.0.windows.3 it prints nothing at all for a repository with changes and exits 0, which is an empty change list indistinguishable from a clean tree -- a dirty project would have fingerprinted clean and every check keyed to it would have gone green. It was caught by a_dirty_project_fingerprints_differently_from_a_clean_one, not by reading the flag list. The prefix is stripped with Path::strip_prefix, not string comparison, so a project in app/ is not confused by a sibling app-old/. A nested checkout that Git reports as one untracked directory is walked and read; a walk that loses something is FingerprintError::IncompleteTree, never a hash of a partial tree; the byte budget is over the whole fingerprint and a file that crosses it is an error, never a prefix hash. ProjectFingerprint::matches compares kind and digest and never id. Gate set: cargo fmt --all -- --check clean; cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings clean; cargo test --workspace --all-features --no-fail-fast = 624 passed, 0 failed, 1 ignored, across 17 test binaries and 4 doc-test targets (553 at P2-T001, +71 = 37 in sure-core lib and the new fingerprint_git target); taskctl validate = state OK: 166 tasks. 20 mutations in target/tmp/mutate6.py, 20 fired. Three of them found real holes in an already-green suite and the tests that close them were written afterwards: (1) Reader::tree -- the whole nested-checkout walk, its per-file path digest and its IncompleteTree guard -- was reached by no test at all; (2) the monorepo test proved only stability, so an implementation that never stripped the prefix, looked every path up at root/prefix/..., found Gone and hashed nothing passed every assertion it made; (3) the byte budget had only ever been exercised with one file, which cannot tell a per-file budget from a per-fingerprint one. The script reports BUILD for a mutation that fails to compile rather than counting it as caught, and SKIP for an anchor that does not match exactly once, after the first version of two mutations were a no-op and a compile failure respectively. NOT VERIFIED ON THIS MACHINE: the three #[cfg(unix)] tests (two link tests and the unreadable-file test) have never run here -- Windows cannot create a symlink without Developer Mode or administrator rights, both probed and absent, and the WSL here has Git 2.53.0 but no cargo. One of the three was rewritten this session without having run anywhere. Their verification is the ubuntu-latest and macos-latest CI jobs, which RUST_DESIGN.md names as the designed path for Unix-only behaviour; the Windows job passing says nothing about them. No dispatcher between Git and content fingerprinting is provided: choosing is P2-T003's decision, and fingerprint/mod.rs says so. HARDENED AFTER ACCEPTANCE: a security review of 9f13f0d found the fingerprint could still be made to run a program the repository chose, and it was right -- the fix was incomplete. A tracked .gitattributes names a filter driver and the repository's own configuration gives it a command, so a plain git status executes it; measured with a marker program and a positive control, and it fires with nothing modified. It cannot be switched off: there is no Git flag that disables in-tree .gitattributes (git help --config lists only the global core.attributesFile), the driver name is not known until Git has read the project so there is no fixed -c to pass, and overriding it anyway would be worse than refusing -- with the filter off Git compares raw bytes against a blob written through the filter and calls every such file modified, a wrong fingerprint rather than an absent one. So the repository is refused, with the new FingerprintError::RepositoryRunsPrograms naming the settings it found. The check is one extra invocation, git -c core.fsmonitor=false --no-pager config --list --includes -z with GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1 and GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=<root>/.git/config/sure-no-global-configuration, run AFTER rev-parse (measured not to run a filter) and BEFORE status (measured to run one -- a check that came after would be a report). That path cannot exist on any platform because .git/config is a file in every repository Git makes, including linked worktrees and submodules, so no project can add settings to the answer about itself. --local is not used and the reason is measured: it does not follow include.path without --includes and misses .git/config.worktree even with it. CORRECTION MADE IN THIS COMMIT: --includes was documented as load-bearing and it is not -- git config --list with no scope named already follows includes, measured after a mutation showed dropping the flag failed only the pinning test and no behavioural test. The flag is kept, the claim is corrected in the source, in FINGERPRINTING.md and in the test. BOUNDARY, MEASURED AND LEFT OPEN: a repository can still reach a filter defined by the MACHINE's config by naming the driver in .gitattributes (target/tmp/boundary_probe.sh, and both C:/Program Files/Git/etc/gitconfig and ~/.gitconfig carry filter.lfs.* here). It is left open because the project cannot choose the program, only ask for one the user installed, which is not project-controlled executable code -- the line EXECUTION_SAFETY.md draws. Documented in FINGERPRINTING.md and raised in HANDOFF.md rather than folded into this fix. 34 mutations in target/tmp/mutate6.py, 34 fired, 8 of them new for this check; the two most valuable are 'the check runs after the status instead of before it', which is caught only by the assertion that the marker does NOT exist, and 'the suppressed global path is one a project could create'.

P2-T003.notes: crates/sure-core/src/fingerprint/content.rs (the manifest), choose.rs (which kind a project gets), read.rs (the path-reading machinery both kinds share: Reader, Contents, file_kind, display_path) + tests/fingerprint_content.rs (23 tests) + tests/fingerprint_git.rs unchanged at 43 + docs/architecture/FINGERPRINTING.md (a content-fingerprint section, the dispatch rule, gaps 8). Acceptance criterion 1, scoped content manifest is deterministic: the manifest is a SHA-256 over the walk's files and links, sorted by the text that goes into the digest rather than by the paths, with the path digested beside the contents so that a move or a name swap is a change. Two copies of one project in two directories agree (two_copies_of_one_project_are_one_fingerprint), which is what proves no absolute path reaches the digest. Every limit -- max_depth, max_entries, max_files, max_bytes -- is an error and never a digest over the part that fitted. Acceptance criterion 2, generated/vendor churn is excluded by documented rules: the walk IS crate::scan, the same tables and the same comparison the checks use, so the exclusion is not a second list that can drift. the_excluded_list_is_the_scans_and_not_a_second_copy_of_it pins the agreement rather than the list; churn_in_every_excluded_kind_of_directory_changes_nothing rewrites one directory per SkipReason (build output, vendored, caches, .venv, .sure) and asserts the digest does not move, with the control that a covered file does move it -- without that control a fingerprint that never moved at all would pass. a_repositorys_own_storage_is_out_so_a_commit_does_not_move_the_manifest makes an empty commit, asserts the ref really moved, and then asserts the manifest did not. The decision this task owned, and it is the reason choose.rs exists rather than a boolean in a caller: a project is fingerprinted by Git when it is at the ROOT of the working tree containing it, not merely inside one. rev-parse --show-prefix is empty exactly then. A directory one level inside somebody else's checkout gets Content, because the Git kind would digest the OUTER repository's HEAD -- a commit anywhere else in that repository moves the subdirectory's fingerprint although not one of its files changed, and evidence marked stale for a project nobody touched is how a person learns to ignore the word. That is measured, both ways, in the_git_kind_moves_for_a_commit_the_project_is_not_part_of_and_the_content_kind_does_not, which also asserts the Git kind still DOES move, so the reason cannot quietly become folklore. A machine without Git is GitUnavailable and NOT a fallback to Content: the kind has to be a function of the project and not of the machine, or one unchanged directory is two fingerprints on two machines and never agrees with itself. A FALSE GREEN THIS TASK FOUND IN ITS OWN TESTS. The first version of the test named a_project_in_no_repository_at_all_is_fingerprinted_by_content used a fixture under target/, which is inside the SURE checkout and therefore inside a working tree -- so it was exercising the 'somebody else's repository' branch and never the 'no repository' one, and it passed. Nothing about the assertion was false and nothing said the fixture could not reach its case. The mutation 'a directory in no repository is refused rather than read by content' was MISSED by every test, which is what surfaced it. Fixed by Fixture::outside_any_repository (the system temp directory) plus git_prefix(), which asserts the premise with git directly -- a premise checked with the code under test is not a premise. The same premise assertion was added to the 'inside somebody else's repository' test. Held by reasoning rather than by a test, and recorded as gap 8 rather than left to look covered: the sort before hashing, and the domain tag. target/tmp/mutate7.py applies 16 mutations, all caught, and reports the two link mutations BLIND on Windows. Removing the sort passes every test, because one run sees one filesystem's order and a digest is a value -- there is nothing for a test to compare two of; setting the tag to the Git kind's also passes every behavioural test, because the two digests cannot collide even with one tag (Git opens with 'head', content with 'manifest'), so the tag is belt and braces over the field structure and is pinned by a constant assertion instead. Two mutations that were MISSED until the script was made to run --test fingerprint_git too: read.rs is shared, and the walk inside a nested directory is only ever reached through the Git kind. The file limit and the byte budget tests were also both boundary-weak and were strengthened: max_files now asserts both sides of three files under limits of three and two, and the byte budget is now shown to be spent by the whole manifest rather than by each file. One earlier claim was corrected rather than quietly dropped: the two-kinds-cannot-collide test comment said it was 'belt and braces over the domain tags', which the mutation showed is not what makes the two digests differ.

Acceptance -- detects Cargo workspaces/packages and conventional commands -- is met by: A Cargo.toml IS A DOCUMENT WITH TWO SIBLING TABLES, `[package]` and `[workspace]`, AND EITHER CAN BE ABSENT. That single fact is what the module is arranged around. A manifest with only `[workspace]` is a virtual manifest, and it declares a great deal -- the members, their shared dependencies, their shared lint levels -- so the workspace tables are held on `Manifest` and NOT on `PackageSection`, and `Manifest` is a separate type for that reason. The first draft hung them off the package, where a virtual manifest's entire workspace, the case such a manifest exists for, would have been dropped; mutation 24 reverts exactly that decision and is caught. A third fact is kept apart from both and is not a convenience: `[dependencies]` is meaningful only where `[package]` exists, because Cargo refuses a virtual manifest that declares dependencies. The same split decides the commands, and this is the second designed-out bug rather than a discovered one: `command_for` gates on `project.manifest.manifest()?` -- the DOCUMENT -- and deliberately not on `package()`. Gating on the package would have withheld every command from a workspace root, which is a project `cargo build` acts on and builds every member of. The comment at that line says so, mutation 23 deletes the gate and is caught, and a test covers the virtual-manifest case directly. Members are resolved by the same `pattern` module Node uses -- one `*` per path segment, lifted into discover/pattern.rs so the two ecosystems cannot come to expand a glob two ways -- and the resolution reports what it could NOT resolve as data rather than dropping it. AN `exclude` LIST IS NOT SUBTRACTED: whether a directory named by both `members` and `exclude` is a member is Cargo's rule and SURE has not read it, so `Workspaces::excluded_members` carries the overlap and neither list is applied. Reporting the overlap is reversible by a reader who knows the rule; silently honouring it would be SURE asserting a rule it cannot cite. Mutation 19 makes `exclude` delete the member and is caught. THE TOOLCHAIN PIN IS READ BY THE FILE'S NAME, because the two names say different amounts: `rust-toolchain.toml` holds a `[toolchain]` table (channel, components, targets, profile) and the bare `rust-toolchain` is not TOML and usually holds one token. `toolchain_from_text` therefore branches on the name and not on what parsed -- a `.toml` that parses but carries no `[toolchain]` table is WrongShape, a `.toml` that does not parse is NotParsed, and only a file that is not TOML falls through to the bare-channel reading. This is the one place a filename changes an answer and the doc says so. Components are matched without regard to case, and `ToolchainState::asks_for("clippy")` answers false for Absent as well as for Unread, so the one question a caller may collapse is the one that collapses to false. Mutation 5, 6 and 7 break the three arms and are all caught; mutation 7's coverage needed a test edit, recorded below. Commands are planned only where the declaration is there: `cargo bench` needs a benchmark target or a benchmark-runner tool, `cargo run` needs a package to run, and mutation 14 plans `cargo bench` unconditionally and is caught. A row exists for EVERY CommandRole whether or not it has a command, because "there is no way to bench this project" is a finding and a missing line is not; a row with no command carries no reasons, and a command names a constant and never anything a project wrote. Tooling comes from a 22-crate table over four ToolRoles, with the finding naming the table's own crate spelling and never the project's. Everything a dependency states is carried as one of four facts rather than collapsed into an Option: Requirement::Stated, FromWorkspace, Unstated, NotReadable -- `foo = { workspace = true }` is not a version in this file, and a spec SURE cannot read is not a dependency that is not there. A SECOND COMMIT COMPLETED THIS TASK RATHER THAN EXTENDING IT, and it exists because the first commit's own tests were wrong twice. A background security review flagged crates/sure-core/src/discover/pattern.rs, the module this task had just lifted out of node.rs. Reading it independently found the containment rule sound -- no traversal, no filesystem reach, no unbounded expansion -- and found the real gap underneath: THE MODULE HAD NO TESTS AT ALL, 209 lines of behaviour that decides which directories SURE reads, reachable through three callers and therefore checked three ways and stated nowhere. Nine tests were added against a real walk (`scan` and `Tree::of`, the same pair production uses, so a walk that changed shape fails here rather than being papered over by a hand-built tree), and a fourth family of mutations (28-34) was anchored on pattern.rs so those tests are shown to be load-bearing rather than counted as coverage: a pattern that climbs out refused in every position, including the two that begin with a directory that genuinely resolves; an absolute pattern refused where the PLATFORM says it is absolute, so `C:\Windows` is refused on Windows and is one ordinary file name on Unix; an unexpandable pattern refused rather than partly expanded; the root named by `.` and never a member of itself; `*` naming directories and never files; two patterns reaching one directory naming it once; a refusal told apart from a pattern that named nothing; the platform's case rule rather than a spelling; and every reason a pattern can fail for being nameable and describable. THE FIRST VERSION OF THOSE TESTS TURNED THE SUITE RED, AND THE MUTATION RUN IS WHAT SAID SO: the scratch helper used the process id, and `discovery_runs_none_of_the_scripts_it_reads` greps the TEXT of all six files in the module tree for the process module's name, `#[cfg(test)]` code included. The suite was therefore failing before any mutation was applied and every CAUGHT in that run was unattributable -- and this is exactly the fault a person checking their own work would miss, because `cargo test --lib discover::pattern` is green either way. The fix is in the test and not in the check, because the check was right about the file: uniqueness now comes from `create_dir` failing rather than from a name, which is strictly stronger, because a process id is unique within one run and says NOTHING across two -- a name built from it collides with a previous run's directory when the OS hands out the same id, and the test then reads a fixture some earlier run had already written into, where `create_dir` refuses to adopt a directory that exists. It then went red a SECOND time, on the sentence explaining the fix: the sentinel searches raw text, so a doc comment reading "no `std::process` here, deliberately" tripped the very check it was describing. A mention is not an ability, and the test now drops whole-line comments before searching -- only whole-line ones, so every line that can hold code is still searched. Neither fault was visible in a diff; both were found by running something that was expected to pass. Both are now rules the harness enforces instead of steps a person remembers: the suite is run UNMUTATED first and a red baseline ends the run with BASELINE IS NOT GREEN, and the compiler-error list is kept separate from the FAILED list so that an error line reaching stdout cannot return CAUGHT for a suite that did not compile. The doc gained six enforced-by rows for the new tests, one rewritten row recording that the no-process check reads source text and drops comments, and a gap 16: an `exclude` pattern that is refused, or that names nothing, leaves no trace. That does NOT misstate membership -- `excluded_members` means "these resolved members are also named by exclude", and an empty list is true in every one of those cases -- but it costs a reader the ability to tell an `exclude` list SURE could not follow from one that named nothing, and the two are worth telling apart because a member list cut off by `max_workspace_members` computes its overlap against the truncated list. The enforced-by index was re-checked mechanically rather than by eye: 88 backticked identifiers, of which 87 are `#[test]` functions and one is a deliberately named function (`read_manifest`), and 0 are found nowhere.
